newsitem.title: KENYA: "Great Lakes" summit to open, boosted by Mandela.
newsitem.headline: "Great Lakes" summit to open, boosted by Mandela.

text.p: A summit on the crisis in central Africa's Great Lakes region opens on Monday with South African President Nelson Mandela taking part in high-level talks on the conflicts in Zaire and Burundi for the first time.
Kenyan officials and South African diplomats in Nairobi said the summit would open at about 3.30 p.m. (1230 GMT) with a speech by host President Daniel arap Moi of Kenya.
Mandela will arrive at 1.30 p.m. (1030 GMT), they said.
About nine heads of state or government were expected at the summit which may continue on Tuesday, they added. It will focus on the search for a ceasefire and political settlement in eastern Zaire.

Rebels there launched a well-planned offensive in mid-October and now control eastern key towns. They say their ultimate goal is to end the 31-year reign of Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko who is due to return to Kinshasa on Tuesday.

The crisis in the Great Lakes -- an area roughly comprising Zaire, Burundi, Rwanda and parts of Tanzania and Uganda -- is potentially the most far-reaching in Africa since the Nigerian civil war in the late 1960s.
As Africa's leading statesman, Mandela has succumbed to international pressure to get directly involved after months of observing from the sidelines.

Zimbabwe's President Robert Mugabe will also attend the summit. The president of Eritrea was the first to arrive on Sunday and other leaders expected are from Ethiopia, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia.
Zaire's senior diplomat in Nairobi told Reuters on Monday he was still unsure whether his country would be at the summit.
Zaire boycotted the first Nairobi summit on the Great Lakes last November 5, refusing to sit down with Rwanda which it accuses of sponsoring the rebellion.
The rebels have not been invited to take part and nor has Burundi's military regime, Kenyan officials say.
An estimated 150,000 people have died since 1993 in ethnic war in Burundi between majority Hutus and minority Tutsis who dominate the armed forces.

The Zaire conflict has pushed Burundi into the background but U.N. human rights monitors say the level of killing has gone on unabated. Some of the leaders expected in Nairobi will argue for the lifting or easing of economic sanctions imposed on Burundi after Major Pierre Buyoya's military coup last July 25.
Last November's summit called in vain for a ceasefire in eastern Zaire and the deployment of a neutral international force to assist 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees caught up in the fighting.
Plans for the force were formally shelved last weekend.
About half the refugees in Zaire returned home peacefully last November and the exact number remaining is disputed.
The second largest concentration of Rwandan Hutu refugees is in Tanzania and a majority of the 500,000 in camps there were flooding back home on Monday.
The Hutus left Rwanda in 1994 after many in their community committed a genocide against Tutsis and pro-opposition Hutus.
